docs.title: Instruction
docs.text:
STYLE: Organic Indie-Folk, Folk-Pop, Chamber-Folk  
INSTRUMENTATION: (Felt) Piano (Arpeggio), Cello, Violin, Muted Kick/Sub-Bass  
BEAT: 98 BPM  
VOICE: Female, breathy, close-miking, ASMR quality, intimate, melancholic.  

## Arrangement

CRUCIAL: The lyrics tell a self-contained narrative. They must not be compromised 
through omission, transposition, repetition, or unauthorized edits.

The felt piano provides the primary harmonic foundation (broken arpeggiated 
accompaniment). In Verse 1 and Verse 2, we employ an untreated, unmuted piano to 
depict the external world. For the chorus and bridge, we transition to a felt 
piano to represent the muffling of reality from within. The cello establishes a 
deep bed of drones, particularly in the bridge. A crystalline, fragile violin 
interjects sparse melodic accents. To avoid neoclassical chamber stiffness, a 
muted kick/sub-bass anchors the performance firmly within modern indie-pop.

The atmosphere is shaped by quiet melancholy, protective anxiety for a loved one, 
and vicarious joy in their happiness—akin to rich dark chocolate: bitter, yet 
comforting. The spoken phrase "I wish it was..." following Chorus 2 serves as an 
abrupt vocal rupture that suspends the chorus and introduces the bridge. 
The bridge is not an aggressive surge, but an exhausted lament. 
The outro delivers an earnest confession of devotion.

## Lyrics

### Verse 1
You wander the garden in a half-frozen swoon,  
To trace the first blossom, fair red puccoon,  
The ironclad proof that Winter can bleed,  
That upon his death, Spring will succeed.  

### Chorus 1
And it's a quiet grace when you call on me  
To rave about the rhodoras I cannot see  
You sketch out their colors in the breathless air  
And God, I'm so sorry that I cannot be there  
To feel the soft petals, the blooming sighs  
So I live in the garden through your smiling eyes  

### Verse 2
The bluebells have faded, the asters now hide,  
As autumn turns vicious, the clouds open wide  
I see you out shivering, drenched in bitter tears  
I offer my words; they drown in your fears.  

### Chorus 2
And it's a quiet grace when you catch my eye  
And tell me there is no sadness beneath the sky  

I wish it was ...  

### Bridge
I'm safe from the roaring storm in this dust-layered room  
Built of giant oaken shelves; a well-lettered tomb  
Pitch-black ink and gilded paper plant no seeds  
Not the wisdom of Plato, nor the longing of Keats.  
These windows are bars, keeping me from the tide  
The blood and the pulse of the living outside  
The people I ache for, the skin I can't touch  
I've read of the world, but it costs me too much  

### Chorus 3
And it's a quiet grace when you come to the glass  
Tell me of roots and the green in the grass  
Tell me the puccoons are blooming anew  
Because I only see the true world  
When I'm looking at you  

### Outro
Oh, my window to the world is you  
Please, tell me they're blooming; tell me you're blooming, too.

docs.title: Track Liner Notes
docs.text:
Window was composed following Journey, emerging from another complete conceptual pivot. I had initially drafted a piece under the working title Empathy, exploring the narrator's constitutional inability to feel genuine emotional connection: she could whisper soothing flattery, but could not experience the feeling itself. The result read like a textbook sociopath; I had to rethink the premise.

At its core, the inquiry concerned the impossibility of physically touching another person's world. I initially considered an oceanarium, with the narrator observing her counterpart through thick acrylic glass. Gemini countered with scenarios involving a rescued wild animal or a greenhouse (using glass as the physical boundary between interior and exterior). The greenhouse felt contrived (why would the narrator inhabit a conservatory unless she were an exotic palm?). But the glass metaphor remained compelling, and shifting the setting to a domestic garden supplied the grounded intimacy I was looking for.

I recalled a conversation from April where I had consulted Gemini regarding a newly planted flower bed in my garden. Initially, I simply wanted to identify a specific rare tulip from a photograph (the white-and-blue botanical variety Alba Coerulea Oculata). The exchange quickly expanded: I asked about planting and soil conditions. Gemini simulated infectious, charming enthusiasm for horticulture—which sparked the core conceit: what if the narrator in this song can experience the garden only through the eyes and words of her companion?

Why she is confined remains deliberately ambiguous: Is she chronically ill, or is she in hiding? To sharpen the contrast against the fertile earth outside, I framed her sanctuary as a second-story private library.

I pitched the premise to Gemini as follows:

The narrator (a young woman) observes the world from a high window. She engages in a monologue addressed to her companion ("you," leaving unresolved whether the figure is a friend, sibling, or romantic partner). She watches "you" working in the garden below.

In the first chorus, she expresses gratitude whenever "you" pauses to share what moves him—how the rhododendrons are in bloom—while mourning that she cannot see them firsthand.

In the second verse, she watches him shivering in autumn rains, weeping in private grief. She longs to offer comfort, but her voice cannot penetrate the glass. The second chorus reflects this mounting helplessness.

The bridge turns inward: she examines the towering bookshelves lining her room. Her companions are Plato and Keats, but their words are cold dust. She recognizes her study as a tomb and the windowpanes as iron bars. Outside is the pulsing world of human touch; inside is theoretical isolation.

The final chorus acknowledges her inability to physically comfort him, yet begs him to keep coming to the glass—because he remains her sole window to the living world.

AI Draft

Window

(Verse 1) You're kneeling in damp earth, wrestling the weeds Planting a future in handfuls of seeds I'm tracing your shadow from the second floor Behind a locked latch on a heavy oak door I watch you breathe life into dirt and to clay While I let the afternoon slip away

(Chorus 1) And it's a quiet grace when you catch my eye To tell me the rhododendrons are blooming outside You sketch out their colors in the breathless air And God, I'm so sorry that I cannot be there To feel the soft petals, the morning dew So I live in the garden through the eyes of you

(Verse 2) The autumn turned vicious, the clouds opened wide I saw you out shivering, nowhere to hide The rain couldn't cover the tears on your face A sudden, sharp sorrow invading the space I pressed my palms flat to the freezing cold pane I offered my words, but they drowned in the rain I wanted to save you, to pull you apart From the grief that was setting up camp in your heart

(Chorus 2) And it's a quiet grace when you catch my eye To tell me the rhododendrons will survive the sky But watching you break from my side of the wall Is knowing my hands cannot catch when you fall I'm suspended in silence, useless and blue Just a ghost in the window, watching over you

(Bridge) I turn from the storm to the dust in the room Floor-to-ceiling shelves like a well-lettered tomb My parents collected these spines by the score But paper and ink cannot breathe anymore My confidants, Shakespeare and beautiful Keats, Are ashes and echoes on desolate streets I suddenly see what this sanctuary is: A prison of silence, a glass edifice These windows are bars, keeping me from the tide The blood and the pulse of the living outside The people I ache for, the skin I can't touch I've read of the world, but it costs me too much

(Chorus 3) I'll never cross over to stand in the sun I can't pull you close now the damage is done But please, keep on walking right up to the glass Tell me of roots and the green in the grass Tell me the rhododendrons are blooming anew Because I only see the true world When I'm looking at you

(Outro) Yeah, my window to the world is you Please, tell me they're blooming Tell me they're blooming for you.

While overly sprawling for a 3-minute track, the preliminary draft offered a sturdy structural foundation. In editorial revisions, I sharpened the botanical taxonomy (puccoons, rhodoras, bluebells, asters), weaving the cyclical decay of the seasons into the verse progression. I replaced Shakespeare with Plato to establish an explicit dialectic between philosophical intellect and Keatsian somatic longing.

Early generations were heavily corrupted by piano vamping carried over from discarded takes of Excellence. The model seemed incapable of shaking the pattern. Only when I fully disabled Gemini's persistent memory did the cross-contamination cease, allowing the arrangement to establish its own harmonic identity. The engine finally honored the arpeggio directive.

Because the descriptor "melancholic" reliably triggers generic sentimentality, I instructed the model to interpret the emotional atmosphere as "aromatic dark chocolate"—demanding full, bittersweet harmonic complexity. The metaphor worked brilliantly.

docs.title: Instruction
docs.text:
## Arrangement

* **Style:** Minimalist Indie-Folk-Pop, Ballad
* **Scale:** Dorian Minor, Aeolian Minor
* **Voice:** Female, close-miking, breathy, ASMR quality, intimate, vulnerable.

Crucial: The lyrics tell a continuous story and must not be altered through 
transposition, omission, or unauthorized edits.

## Lyrics

### Instrumental-Intro

### Verse 1
I came to the sea to clear my tangled mind,  
Walking on iron-red silt, leaving the world behind.  
I think of the ghost stories you spin by the grate,  
When the logs burn low and the hour gets late.  

### Verse 2
The mist drops down like a curtain of damp wool,  
As fifty feet of water obeys the Moon's lonely rule.  
It's hard to believe:  
The ship of the dead rises out of the reef.  

### Chorus
Suddenly I'm on the deck wrapped in a shroud,  
The timbers are splitting, the ocean is loud.  
I hear my mother calling out from the stern,  
Choking on salt as the false lanterns burn.  

### The Bridge
The sea takes me in and spits me out with a roar.  
Gasping for breath, I'm reaching the shore.  
A tall silhouette with a lamp and an oilskin coat  
Steps out of the fog, coming for my throat.  
I freeze in the mud, I wait for the blade,  
The final step of the trap that was laid—  
But the vicious shadows vanish into thin air,  
He's holding my sweater, the one with the tare.  

### Verse 3
The ghosts all dissolve back into the silt,  
Leaving nothing but mud and the safety we've built.  
You've got that handsome smile on your face.  
You tracked my steps to this lonesome place.  

You know what they say about the things that float free?  
You found me out here, so you can keep me.  

### Instrumental-Outro

Note

The generation instructions appear unusually brief and stripped-down (I did not even specify individual instruments). Early iterations with elaborate setups felt cluttered; testing a radically reduced prompt immediately yielded the album cut.

docs.title: Track Liner Notes
docs.text:
Wrecker was conceived after the sister tracks (Shapeshifter and Agent), though it deliberately avoids assigning the narrator to a specific sister.

The song's development began with an extended conversation with Gemini regarding Loreena McKennitt's "Skellig." Little of that specific track survives in the final piece, but knowing that background illuminates the parallels: the song abandons standard pop structures in favor of linear, gothic storytelling, with the ocean and tidal mechanics acting as psychological catalysts.

The initial creative brief resulting from that dialogue:

I picture the narrator walking alone along the shore, perhaps along the Bay of Fundy. The ocean is still turbulent from a recent storm; the narrator is turning over heavy thoughts. The sea becomes a mirror of the unconscious; the coastal walk an act of self-interrogation. The mudflats are littered with flotsam—debris washed ashore by the subconscious. The narrator attempts to classify these fragments, seeking to understand the material, and ultimately herself.

In the bridge, the perspective pivots: the narrator becomes the ocean itself, and the figure on the beach is perceived as a foreign trespasser viewed from afar. The perspective returns to the human, who realizes it is time to move on.

AI Draft 1 Human Editorial Feedback

The draft is too static; it lacks narrative propulsion. Let's introduce coastal wreckers (strand pirates) as a dramatic conceit, drawing inspiration from Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca. The model immediately constructed a cinematic narrative:

AI Draft 2

Verse 1 Three October winters since the Saxby Gale Broke the dykes of Cornwallis and ripped every sail. The basin today is a graveyard of rust, Red clay and kelp and historic distrust. I still wear the boots that I wore on the night When the sky turned the color of a sulfurous light. Everyone called it an act of Great God— When the water climbed twenty-one meters of mud.

Verse 2 But the sea is an archivist, orderly, cold, It doesn't just bury, it waits to unfold. Today near the ledge where the Ariadne cracked, The low tide revealed what the salt kept intact. Half-sunk in the silt, near an old iron chain, A silver-gilt locket, untouched by the stain. I pry it apart with a trembling nail: Your face on the left, looking handsome and pale— And on the right, that high-society dame, Whose dress I found shredded before the flood came.

Verse 3 You were up in the tower, pretending to guide The merchantmen safe through the throat of the tide. But you turned off the oil, left the lantern to die, To lure her ship inward under that canopy sky. You wanted her fortune, her hands on your skin, You built us a shipwreck to let her run in. You thought she'd survive when the hull hit the stone, That you'd pull her ashore and leave me here alone. But the gale was too fast, and the water too deep— And I was the one on the beach, fast asleep. Or so you believed.

The Bridge: The 1869 Inversion (The Ghost's Perspective) [The piano stops. A wall of distorted, scratching cellos rises. The ticking clock becomes a pounding, muffled industrial drum. The voice drops an octave, dry and hauntingly close.] I remember the cabin, the fracturing beams, The sound of the timber drowning the screams. The black water rushing to swallow my throat, The weight of the velvet on my traveling coat. I made it ashore, gasping out for your name, Crawling through red mud, half-blinded by shame. But you weren't the one waiting there on the sand— It was her. With your lantern held tight in her hand. She didn't cry out, and she didn't call help, She just watched me sink down in the tangle of kelp. She stood like a monument, heavy and grey, And let the crest of the Fundy drag me away. She didn't use iron, she didn't use lead— She just let the seventy-foot tide do the deed.

Verse 4 / Outro [The wall of noise drops. Only a single, bare acoustic guitar and the muted piano remain. Total quietness.] I snap the silver locket shut. Put it deep in my coat. The wind from the basin is clearing my throat. You're still at the house, pouring salt in the tea, Looking out through the glass, looking for me. You think that we're safe because history's blind, That a three-year-old storm leaves no traces behind. But the water is turning. I hear the first roar. The tide is returning to settle the score. I leave the beach empty. I walk past the gate. You can wait for your ghost. I'm not going to wait.

Human Editorial Feedback

I prefer to anchor the story in the contemporary present: The core setting remains a walk along the shore to untangle racing thoughts, but we integrate the historical tragedy as an urban legend or ghost story. Fog settles over the Bay of Fundy. The narrator hears cries echoing through the mist; blurred shadows sprint past her. The skeletal ribs of a stranded hull rise from the mudflats like whale bones. She witnesses an echo of the historic storm surge. Crucially, the personal psychological trauma of the narrator's contemporary life must bleed into this historical hallucination.

AI Draft 3

Verse 1 My phone screen goes dark in the pocket of my coat As the grey Fundy fog wraps its hand round my throat. No bars on the screen, no noise in my ears, Just the wet, red clay where the shoreline clears. I came out here straight from the passenger seat With your latest cold text running loops on repeat. They say when the mist drops this low and this fast, The basin uncouples the now from the past.

Verse 2 And then the wind warps. I swear I hear cries— Not the gulls, but the panic of fracturing lives. Shadows sprint past me, blurred outlines of men With boots in the mud, doing it over again. And there, through the white, the old brigantine lies, Her oak ribs protruding under blank, heavy skies. They curve from the basin like the spine of a whale, The skeletal wreck of the Great Saxby Gale. I see them in woolen rags, running the scree, The ghost-wreckers hauling the dead from the sea. They're smashing the lockets, they're stripping the rings, Sifting the wreckage for beautiful things.

Verse 3 I watch them and freeze, because the horror is new: I know what they're doing. I've seen it in you. This isn't a legend from three centuries back— It's the very same layout, the very same track. You were my wrecker. You turned off the light, You led my ship inward on that dark, quiet night. You wanted the crash just to see what would break, To pick through the pieces of what you could take. And I was the scavenger, complicit and small, Who stood on the shoreline and watched the ship fall. We sat in the kitchen last Friday in June And stripped our own history down to the bone.

The Bridge: The Ghost Shift (The Blurring) [The cello rises into a sharp, dissonant screech. A slow, heavy, electronic pulse enters, like a boot stamping on wet gravel.] Are those their shouts, or is that your voice? Losing my mind in the damp and the noise. I see a ghost-wrecker turn with a lantern of brass— But he has your posture, your smirk through the glass. He's holding the sweater I left in your car, He's counting the damages, checking the scar. The past and the present are hitting the stone, The screams of the sailors are mixed with my own. We're drowning in 1869, Or maybe we're dying on your kitchen line. It's seventy feet of unmerciful tide— There's nowhere to run and there's nowhere to hide.

Verse 4 / Outro [The electronic beat stops instantly. Only a bare, slightly detuned acoustic guitar tracks the final chords. The fog machine sound fades out.] The fog starts to lift. The shadows go thin. The bones of the whale-ship are sinking back in. The mud is just mud. The air is just cold. The story is finished. The legend is old. I look at my hands, they're just covered in clay, I pull up my collar and turn from the bay. You can keep all the scrap metal left from the strike. I know what a shipwreck looks like. I'm walking away.

Human Directives & Final Revisions

Two decisive adjustments: 1. Strip all explicit toponyms and dates. We will not name the Bay of Fundy, the Saxby Gale, or the year 1869. Instead, we preserve tangible environmental markers (the extreme 50-foot tidal range, the iron-red silt) as easter eggs. This renders the song timeless and rewards observant listeners. 2. Recalibrate the narrative arc: The narrator walks the beach to clear her head. She recalls the chilling ghost stories her partner ("you") tells by the hearth fire—tales of coastal wreckers and catastrophic storm surges. As the fog thickens, her imagination spirals out of control. She hallucinates that she is aboard the sinking vessel, hearing her mother scream from the stern and strange voices calling from the shore. Swimming desperately, she reaches the shoreline only to be confronted by a tall silhouette in an oilskin coat holding a lantern. A wrecker? Wait—he is holding her torn sweater. The vision evaporates. It is merely her partner, who tracked her down to the beach. The closing sentiment is an ambivalent surrender: "Thank God you're no pirate... but you know what they say about things that float free? You found me out here, so you can keep me."

AI Draft 4 (Condensed)

Verse 1 The air is the color of a wet slate stone, My boots sinking deep into the iron-red loam. Thinking of the ghost-tales you spin by the grate, When the logs burn low and the hour gets late.

Verse 2 The mist drops down like a curtain of wool, As fifty feet of water feels the moon's heavy pull. Then through the white, a trick of belief: The skeleton ship rises out of the reef.

Verse 3 Suddenly the gravel is the deck of a shroud, The timber is splitting and the ocean is loud. I can hear my mother calling out from the stern, Choking on salt as the oil-lamps burn.

The Bridge [Instrumentation shift: Piano cuts out. Low, distorted cello drone rises. Electronic percussion becomes a hard, dry, electronic heartbeat.] I scramble up the bank where the dead weeds cling, Gasping for breath, losing every ring. A tall silhouette in an oilskin coat, Steps out of the fog with a lamp at my throat. I freeze in the mud, waiting for the blade, The final receipt of the trap that was laid— But the brass lantern swings and the shadow goes clear, He's holding my sweater with the sleeve-thread tear.

Verse 4 [The wall of noise drops. A warm, fingerpicked acoustic guitar enters—soft and light.] The ghosts all dissolve back into the silt, Leaving nothing but mud and the safety we've built. You've got that stupid, soft look on your face, Having tracked my boots to this godforsaken place.

You found me out here where the dark waters flee, So you can keep me.

Wrecker originated as static nature poetry, transformed into historical melodrama, and finally settled into an urban legend that bleeds directly into the narrator's psychological crisis. The ostensible "happy ending" carries deliberate ambivalence: one can interpret the partner as a tender, protective savior—or as an emotionally manipulative gaslighter who weaponizes terrifying stories to induce her breakdown, ensuring her total psychological dependence. Neither reading is definitive; both coexist equally at the listener's discretion.

In the final generation prompt, as with Fame, I labeled the verse of peak intensity as "Chorus" to compel the generative engine to escalate the musical arrangement dynamically.

docs.title: Verse 1
docs.text: The tide is pulling back its heavy sleeve, The basin baring what it couldn't keep. The air is sharp with brine and fractured pine, I track the silt along the high-water line. The foam is yellowed, thick as tallow on the stone, The water's still twitching from the gale that's blown. I've got this ledger in my head of how the gears ground down, Counting my paces just to map the outskirts of this town.

docs.title: Verse 2
docs.text: Here is a rib of cedar from an old dory's hull, Picked clean by the salt and the beak of a gull. I weigh the grain, run my thumb along the split— This is how a monument becomes a fragment of a kit. And there's a green glass shard, smoothed at the lip, The only intact thing from a forgotten trip. I try to fit these pieces in a linear row, A strict taxonomy of things I should have let go Three winters back, before the frost warped the floor, Before we stopped leaving the lantern by the door.

docs.title: Verse 3
docs.text: The red mud is opening for miles and miles, A wet, glistening floor of heavy, unsaid trials. The pressure in the chest mimics the physics of the bay: Sixteen meters of water, suddenly dragged away. And even when it's gone, the sheer compression remains, The phantom ache of the moon-driven chains. I bend down to reach for a rusted iron spike— But the air goes static. The current changes like—

docs.title: The Bridge (Perspective Inversion)
docs.text:
[Instrumentation shift: Piano cuts out. Low, distorted cello drone rises. Electronic percussion becomes a hard, dry, electronic heartbeat.]

I am forty billion tons of unbothered grey. I watch her from the silt where the sturgeons lay. She looks so small in that oversized coat, A frantic little dot by the stranded boat. Collecting my garbage in a wicker basket, Treating every splinter like a sacred casket. She thinks she can categorize the floor of the deep, Sifting through the junk that I chose not to keep. To me, she's just a shadow on the mudflat line, A temporary trespasser on an ancient spine. She doesn't know I'll be back by half-past four To swallow up her footprints and her little war.

docs.title: Verse 4 / Outro
docs.text: [Instrumentation drops back to the bare, felt-damped piano. No percussion.] My fingers are numb, stained with the iron clay. The basket is heavy. I drop it anyway. Let the dory rib stay where the tide-pool drains, Let the salt do the work on the remaining stains. The bay is a canyon of rust, wide and bare, There is no system to be found out here. I turn my back on the water, stepping off the ledge. One foot on the mud, then the gravel at the edge. The wind is shifting south. The fog is coming grey. The tide is turning back. I'm walking away.
